newsitem.title: USA: USA: FEATURE-At 94, once-reviled architect has outlived critics.
newsitem.headline: USA: FEATURE-At 94, once-reviled architect has outlived critics.

text.p: If it is true that he who laughs last laughs best, architect Morris Lapidus, 94, is enjoying a long and satisfying chuckle.

The legendary hotel designer, reviled in the 1950s and 1960s as a crass, commercial "High Priest of High Kitsch," has come into his own in the 1990s, with exhibits and books in Europe and the United States and a popular new autobiography.

"That's the one thing that I'm eternally grateful for, that I've lived to see my work accepted. So many architects die and their work is accepted and praised long after they're gone. Architects, artists, writers, musicians, they don't live to get the proper credit for their work," he told Reuters in an interview. "I'm very fortunate."

Born in Russia in 1902, Lapidus came to the United States as an infant. He made his reputation in the 1930s and 1940s as a successful store designer, pioneering shopfronts with large curving windows designed to eliminate the gap between street and store shelves and draw customers inside.

But he found fame and notoriety as the designer of Miami Beach's giant "pleasure palace" hotels, most notably the mid-1950s Fontainebleau and Eden Roc, internationally popular resort spots that attracted American celebrities such as Joe DiMaggio, Elizabeth Taylor and Frank Sinatra.

Lapidus designed curvaceous, decorated buildings rejected by an architectural establishment enamoured with the "international style" of stark glass-and-steel boxes. In a typical comment, British architect Sir Basil Spence, who designed Coventry Cathedral, said of a Lapidus design, "As I approached the hotel, I thought it would bite me."
STAIRWAY TO NOWHERE

The Fontainebleau's oxymoronic "modern French Provincial" interior included a stairway to nowhere, arches, chandeliers, marble, a blowup of a Piranesi etching, latticework, statues and Lapidus's trademark "woggle" and "cheesehole" cutouts.
"I finally realised that American taste was being influenced by the greatest mass media of entertainment of that time, the movies ... so I designed a movie set," Lapidus wrote in his autobiography.

Travel writers loved the Fontainebleau and the public flocked to the hotel. But architecture magazines refused to write about it, saying it was too far outside the mainstream to warrant their attention.

"When I designed the building for which I am famous, the Fontainebleau Hotel, I was rejected and shunned by all the architecture magazines and all the critics," Lapidus said. "I was really banned as an architect."

But his business boomed in spite of the criticism, with commissions in Florida, New York, the Caribbean, Washington, London, Nigeria and Israel. The Fontainebleau remains one of Miami Beach's most popular hotels and the city has just spent millions to renovate Lapidus's outdoor Lincoln Road mall.
Architectural historians said it made sense that the public embraced Lapidus's style, whether or not it was a hodgepodge of periods and materials, since the alternative was stark glass boxes.
PEOPLE WERE TIRED OF 'GOOD' ARCHITECTURE

"It (his work) came along at a time when everything that had been regarded as canonical modern architecture -- all the stuff that the Museum of Modern Art called 'good' -- people had gotten a little tired of," said architectural historian Vincent Scully, who teaches at Yale University and the University of Miami.

"He didn't seem serious enough, or theoretical enough, or disciplined enough to be a great modern architect. But that was kind of a humourless time and it had these kind of very strict codes, you could only do things one way," Scully said.

In 1970, the New York Architectural League's decision to mount a major exhibit on Lapidus' work, "The Architecture of Joy," prompted a debate in which Lapidus was both damned and praised for designing buildings that appealed to the public. In a review of the show, New York Times architecture critic Ada Louise Huxtable slammed Lapidus' work as "uninspired superschlock."

But interest in his work grew, with more exhibitions, speeches and, finally, books and lecture tours. "Morris seemed to have a very special sort of life of his own, we began to look at him again," Scully said.
Lapidus makes no apologies for his hotels, which were intended for people on vacation escapes from day-to-day reality, an attitude reflected in his autobiography's title: "Too Much is Never Enough."

"Architecture is a banquet and too many architects are not starving to death but they are not doing the kind of work that I like and did," he said. "For instance, if you like ice cream why stop at one scoop? Have two, have three. Too much is never enough."
